transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, so I came in because... well, I drive a taxi. It's how I make my money right now since I finished high school, and I'm trying to study on the side, but things have just gotten really, really bad lately. 

See, every time I take the cab out, I have to do this standard safety check, right? Walk around the car, check the lights, the tires, all that. And I do it. I know for a fact I did it. But then... it's like this thought just keeps hitting me out of nowhere. It just crashes into my head that I missed something on the cab. Like, maybe I didn't look closely enough at the brakes or something. And then my brain just spirals, and I start thinking that somebody is gonna get seriously hurt because of my mistake, or my boss is gonna check the car and say I lied on the inspection sheet and fire me. 

And the worst part is, I just can't make it shut up. I'll be driving down the street with a fare in the back, or I'll be sitting at my desk trying to study, and the thought is just playing on a loop, telling me I missed something and it's all going to go wrong. It's exhausting, honestly, just having this constant noise in my head that I can't turn off.
Do these thoughts about missing something on the cab feel like they are coming from outside of yourself, or are they more like your own worries?

Um, no, it's... it's definitely me. It's not like, you know, I'm hearing voices from outside or like someone is beaming things into my brain or anything like that. It's my own voice. It's just my own worries, but it's like they're completely on overdrive, you know? 

Like, I'll be sitting there at a red light—maybe downtown where the traffic is always just completely backed up and I've got a guy in the back seat tapping his foot, checking his watch—and it's my own internal monologue that just suddenly goes, "Hey, did you actually look at the left rear tire, or did you just walk past it?" And I know I looked at it. I know I did. But my own brain just starts arguing with me. It's like I'm fighting with myself. I'll be trying to reason with it, like, "Yes, I checked it at 6:00 AM before I pulled out of the lot, I kicked it, it was fine," and then my brain just fires back with, "Yeah, but did you look close enough? What if there was a nail you missed? What if it blows out on the highway?" 

So it's definitely coming from inside my own skull, which honestly almost makes it worse, if I'm being real with you. Because it's like... why am I doing this to myself? Why can't I just be a normal nineteen-year-old and drive the cab and go home and study without my own mind sabotaging my entire day? It's just me in there, but it's like this version of me that just absolutely refuses to let anything go, no matter how much I try to tell myself everything is fine.
Are these thoughts and worries affecting your relationships with friends or family, or are you able to keep them separate?

Well, yeah, it's... it's really bleeding into everything. I mean, my relationships are definitely taking a hit, but it's not just that, it's my whole life. Like, my friends, they used to call me to hang out on weekends, or even just grab a burger after a shift, but lately I just... I barely see them anymore. I mean, I can't. Half the time I'm so far behind on my work schedule because of all the time I spend checking the car, or I'm just completely exhausted from dealing with it all day. 

And work... man, work is getting bad. I've actually lost rides because I'm just standing there in the lot staring at the tires or the headlights, and I've gotten warnings from dispatch because I can't get on the road on time. They're like, "Where are you? Your shift started twenty minutes ago," and I'm just... I'm stuck. I can't leave the lot until I feel like I've checked it enough. And then, because my work takes so long, I'm trying to catch up all day, which means I have zero energy left when I get home. 

I'm supposed to be studying for my CDL—my commercial driver's license—so I can maybe get a better job, drive trucks or something, you know? Something that pays more than driving a cab around the city. But my studying just keeps getting pushed back and pushed back. I'll sit down with the manual, and my brain is still just screaming about whether I locked the cab doors properly or if the parking brake was pulled up all the way, and I end up reading the same paragraph like five times without absorbing a single word. So much of my day just gets completely eaten up by this... this routine, or whatever you want to call it. So, yeah, it's definitely not just something I can keep separate. It's kind of ruining my friendships, my job, my studying... pretty much everything.
Do you feel like you have to perform the safety check in a specific way or a certain number of times to try to stop these worrying thoughts?

Yeah. Yeah, exactly. It's... it's not just a quick walk-around like they taught us in training. It's this whole... process. And it has to be perfect. 

Like, before I can even take a single ride, before I even turn the key in the ignition, I have to go around the car. And I check the tires, right? I have to physically press on each one, check the tread, make sure there's no nails. Then the lights. Headlights, brights, blinkers, brake lights, reverse lights. Then the doors—I have to open and slam each one to make sure it latches properly. Then I check the meter, make sure it's zeroed out, make sure the paper roll is full. Then the paperwork in the glovebox, the registration, the insurance. 

And I do it over and over. I'll finish the loop, and my brain will just be like, "Did you really check the back left door? Are you sure?" And so I have to do the whole thing again. Sometimes... sometimes I even take pictures with my phone. Like, I'll take a picture of the tire, or a video of me pulling on the door handle, just so I have proof. But even then, if I'm looking at the video and it just doesn't... feel right, you know? Like if I didn't pull the handle hard enough in the video, or if the lighting is weird and I can't clearly see the tire tread... I have to delete the video and start the entire check all over again from the beginning. 

And I'll be doing this, just looping around the cab, and there will literally be passengers standing on the curb waiting for me. Like, I can see them looking at me, getting annoyed, checking their phones. And I'm already late, I'm already behind schedule, dispatch is probably going to yell at me again, but I just... I can't stop. I can't get in the car and drive until the check feels exactly right, no matter how many times I have to do it or who's watching me. It's like I'm trapped in my own parking space.
Do you feel like these thoughts and behaviors are causing you significant distress or are interfering with your daily life in a major way?

Yeah, I mean... absolutely. Like I was kind of getting into earlier, it's... it's basically taking over my entire life. The distress is... well, it's overwhelming, honestly. I just feel so stuck. 

Like, I mentioned the warnings from dispatch, right? It's not just a quick "hey, hurry up" over the radio. I've literally lost rides. Good rides, too, like long airport runs that actually pay well. I'll be stuck in the lot, doing my checking loop for the third or fourth time, trying to get the video of the door handle just right, and dispatch will call my number, and I just have to sit there and listen to another driver take my fare because I can't get on the road on time. That's money right out of my pocket, you know? It's my livelihood. And my boss is starting to look at me like I'm completely unreliable, which just adds to the stress of it all.

And then because I'm losing time and money, I'm constantly trying to catch up. So my CDL studying... the thing that's supposed to be my ticket out of driving this cab... it just keeps getting pushed back and pushed back. I'll finally get home, sit at my desk, open the commercial driving manual, but so much of my day has already been eaten up by this... this endless checking routine, that my brain is just completely fried. I'll stare at the page about air brakes or weight limits or whatever, and I'm just exhausted. I can't retain anything. 

And that totally bleeds into my social life, too. I barely see my friends anymore. They'll text me on a Friday night to hang out, and I just... I can't do it. I'm either still out on the road because I'm behind on my shift from all the checking delays, or I'm at home desperately trying to catch up on the studying I missed, or honestly, I'm just too drained to even pretend to be normal around them. I just make up excuses now. I'll tell them I picked up an extra shift or I'm not feeling well. I can't exactly tell them I spent forty-five minutes kicking a tire, you know? So, yeah, to answer your question, it's a major interference. It really feels like I'm just watching my life pass me by while I'm stuck walking in circles around a taxi.
Would you say that these thoughts about missing something on the cab are unwanted and pop into your mind without you intentionally thinking about them?

Oh, completely. I definitely do not want them there. Honestly, that's the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. I never sit down and try to conjure this stuff up. It just... it ambushes me. 

Like, I'll be driving, right? Just cruising down 4th Avenue, maybe I've got a fare in the back heading to the airport, the radio is on, I'm just looking at the traffic lights. And then, bam. Out of nowhere, this thought just hits me that I missed something on the cab. And the crazy part is, it happens even when I *know* I did my safety check. Like, I know I did it, I probably did it five times and have the video on my phone to prove it, but my brain just ignores all that and starts screaming at me anyway. 

It'll just pop in and be like, "Are you sure the lug nuts were tight? Because if they aren't, the wheel is going to fly off into the crosswalk and somebody could get seriously hurt." Or if it's not that, it's about work. It'll tell me that my boss is going to randomly inspect the car, he's going to see I missed a bald spot on the tire or a cracked taillight, and he's going to say I lied on my pre-trip report. 

And once that thought pops into my head, I just... I can't make it shut up. I try, you know? I try to shake my head, I'll turn the radio up louder, I try to force myself to focus on the road, but it's just playing on a loop, blaring in my mind the entire time I'm driving. And it's the exact same thing when I'm at home. Like I was saying about trying to study for my CDL... I'll be staring right at the manual, trying to memorize weight limits or something, completely trying to focus, and suddenly my brain is just hijacking me with all these scenarios about people getting injured or my boss calling me a liar. I just can't turn it off. It just forces its way in.
Are you doing the safety checks to prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah. Yeah, exactly, 100%. That's... that's the whole reason I do it. Like I was explaining earlier with my whole routine... before I can even take a single ride, I keep going around the car, checking the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, the paperwork, just over and over again. I'm doing all of that specifically because I feel like if I don't, it's an absolute guarantee that something terrible is going to happen. 

I mean, think about it from my perspective. If I don't do the loop, if I don't physically press on the tread and take those pictures of the tires to prove there's no nail, I'll just be picturing a blowout on the interstate the entire time I'm driving. Or the doors—if I don't slam them and get it on video to prove they latched, I'll start thinking a passenger is going to lean against the door and just fall out into moving traffic. And the paperwork, too... if I don't check the glovebox, I'll be convinced I'm going to get pulled over, get a massive ticket, and get fired, which ruins my chances of ever getting my CDL. 

So, yeah, it's all about trying to stop those disasters. That's why, even when there are passengers literally standing right there on the curb, looking at their watches and getting visibly angry with me, and even when I know I'm already late and dispatch is going to chew me out, I still have to keep checking. I can't just get in and drive. If I take a picture or a video and it doesn't feel exactly right, I have to delete it and restart the whole check from the very beginning. Because if I just drove off without being completely, one-hundred-percent sure that I prevented every possible bad thing... the guilt would just eat me alive. I feel like I'm the only one standing between a normal shift and a complete catastrophe, you know? So I just keep checking.
Do you feel less anxious or worried after completing your safety checks?

Yeah, I do... for a minute, anyway. It's like... okay, like I was telling you a second ago about my routine. Before I can even take a single ride, I have to keep going around the car, right? Checking the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, the paperwork, just over and over again. And I'm taking those pictures and videos on my phone. If I get through all of that, and I look at the picture and it finally feels right... then yeah, it's like this massive weight just lifts right off my chest. The panic just kind of drains out of me, and I can actually breathe for a second. 

But getting to that point is just so exhausting. Because, like I was saying, if I take a picture and something just feels even a tiny bit off in my head, I have to restart the whole check from the very beginning. I'll be out there doing the whole loop again, even when passengers are literally waiting right there on the sidewalk. I had this one guy last week, he was standing there with his suitcase, just glaring at me, looking at his watch, sighing super loud, and I knew I was already late and dispatch was going to be furious with me. But I still had to restart the whole check of the doors and the lights and the meter and everything. I couldn't just stop and let him in, because the anxiety would have been unbearable. I had to finish the routine to make the worry stop. 

So, yes, completing it does make me feel less anxious, absolutely. It's the only thing that works. It's just that I have to go through hell, piss off my passengers, and ruin my schedule just to get that tiny little window of relief, you know? And then as soon as I drop that fare off, the whole thing just starts all over again.
Do you feel like you have no choice but to perform these safety checks?

Zero choice. None at all. It's not like I'm just deciding to be overly thorough, you know? It's like... it's like my brain has a gun to my head. 

I know I've brought up the routine a bunch of times today, but I really want you to understand that I literally cannot stop myself. Before I can take a single ride, I just keep going around the car, checking the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, the paperwork, just over and over again. And it's not a choice. If I could just hop in the driver's seat, turn the key, and pull out into traffic like a normal 19-year-old guy, I would. God, I would love to just do that. But I physically can't put the car in drive until it's done. 

I'll be out there, and I'll take a picture of the tire tread or a video of the door latch, and if the lighting is weird, or my hand shook even a millimeter, or if it just doesn't give me that exact right feeling in my gut... I'm trapped. I have no say in the matter. I have to delete the picture and restart the whole check from the very beginning. 

And I think that's the biggest proof that I don't have a choice, right? Because I'm doing this even when passengers are literally standing right there waiting for me. Like I was saying earlier, they'll be tapping their feet, crossing their arms, looking at me like I'm an absolute freak. And I know I'm already late. I know dispatch is going to scream at me over the radio, I'm watching my tips completely vanish, and I'm risking getting fired before I even get my CDL. I'm totally aware of all of that happening in real-time. I'll be sweating, feeling like a total idiot, wanting to just apologize and let them in, but my body just keeps doing the loop. I just have to keep checking. It really feels like I'm a hostage in my own body.
Are you trying to prevent something specific from happening when you do these safety checks?

Yeah, exactly. I know I keep bringing up the exact same routine, and I probably sound like a broken record at this point, but it's because every single part of that check has its own specific disaster attached to it in my head. It's not just some vague worry, you know? 

Like, when I'm doing that loop before I can take a ride... when I'm checking the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, and the paperwork over and over again? I'm picturing very specific, horrible things. With the tires, I'm not just checking them to be safe—I'm specifically seeing a blowout happening at 70 miles an hour on the interstate, the cab flipping over, and my passenger getting crushed. With the doors, I'm terrified that if I don't check the latches perfectly, some little kid is going to lean against the door and just tumble out into moving traffic. The lights... if I don't check the brake lights, I'm picturing a semi-truck rear-ending us and causing a massive pileup. And then the meter and the paperwork... I'm specifically trying to prevent getting pulled over, getting arrested for some technicality, losing my job, and completely destroying any chance I have of ever getting my CDL to drive big rigs. 

So, I mean, when you have those specific images playing on a loop in your brain like a movie, you can't just ignore them. That's why I keep going around the car. That's why I'm taking those pictures and videos on my phone. And if I look at the picture of the tire tread and the lighting is weird, or if I shut the door and it just doesn't feel right in my gut, I have to delete the picture and restart the whole check from the very beginning. I have to. Because if I don't, it feels like I'm basically choosing to let one of those specific disasters happen. 

And it's just... it's so incredibly stressful because I'm doing all of this even when passengers are literally waiting for me right there on the curb. I'll be out there restarting the whole check of the tires and the doors, and I can see them out of the corner of my eye, tapping their phones, getting super pissed off. I know I'm already late. I know my dispatcher is going to scream at me. But I'm trapped. I have to make sure those specific terrible things don't happen before I can let them in the car.
Is the thought of making a mistake on the safety check itself what's driving your anxiety, or is it more about the potential consequences of something going wrong?

It's... I guess it's kind of both, but it all starts with just the thought itself. I mean, honestly, that's the whole reason I finally came in to get help in the first place. Because even when I know for an absolute fact that I did my safety check—like, I have the photos on my phone, I know I did the whole routine perfectly—this thought just keeps hitting me anyway. It just slams into my head out of nowhere that I missed something on the cab. 

And then, yeah, it immediately spirals right into those consequences. I start obsessing that because I missed something, somebody could get seriously hurt, or my boss is going to look at the logs and say I lied about doing the check at all and fire me on the spot. 

But it's the thought itself that's the real torture, because I just... I can't make it shut up. It just gets stuck on a loop. I'll be driving down the road, actually trying to do my job and get someone to their destination safely, and my brain is just screaming at me the entire time that I messed up the inspection and we're in danger. Or I'll be sitting in my room at night, trying to study for my CDL—which is my whole dream, you know, getting my commercial license so I don't have to drive a taxi forever—and I'll be staring at the training manual, but I can't even read the words on the page. The thought is just hammering away at me, over and over. "You missed something, you missed something, someone's going to get hurt, your boss knows you lied." It doesn't even matter that I literally just proved to myself the car was safe. The thought just takes over completely, and it's so loud I can't focus on driving or studying or anything else.
Are there any areas of your life where you feel like you're able to function normally without being affected by these thoughts and safety checks?

Normally? Man, I wish. I really, really wish I could say yes, like, maybe work is a nightmare but at least when I go home I can just chill out like a regular guy. But no, it’s... it literally bleeds into every single corner of my life. There is no "normal" area left. 

I mean, just look at my job. Like I was saying, I've actually lost rides—passengers just canceling on me and taking an Uber instead—and I've gotten official warnings from dispatch because I physically cannot get on the road on time. I'll be scheduled to start my shift, and an hour will go by, and I'm still in the lot, stuck in that loop with the tires and the doors. So work is a total disaster right now. 

And because work takes so much longer, everything else gets ruined, too. Like my CDL studying. Getting my commercial license is my whole goal, it's the only way I'm going to make real money and get out of driving a cab, but my studying just keeps getting pushed back, day after day. So much of my day just gets completely eaten up by these checking delays that by the time I actually have a second to sit down with the manual, the day is over and my brain is fried. 

And as for, like, a social life? Forget it. I barely see my friends anymore. They'll text me to hang out, play games, whatever, and I almost always have to blow them off. I can't go because I'm either way behind on my work quota and trying to grind out rides late into the night to make up for it, or I'm just desperately trying to catch up on everything else in my life after losing hours to the checking. It just takes everything from me. It takes all my time. There's just no part of my day that it doesn't completely take over, you know?
Do you feel like you need things to be symmetrical or just right when you're doing your safety checks?

Yeah, I mean, I kind of touched on that a minute ago, but yes, absolutely. It is one hundred percent about that feeling. It has to feel exactly right, or I can't move on. Like I was saying before about my routine before I can take a ride... I keep going around the car, checking the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, and the paperwork over and over again, right? Well, the reason I get stuck doing it over and over is exactly because of that "just right" thing you just mentioned. 

If I take a picture of the tire tread, for example, and my hand shakes even a tiny bit, or the streetlamp casts a weird shadow across the rubber, it doesn't feel right. Or the doors—man, the doors are the absolute worst. If I shut the back passenger door and it doesn't make this specific, solid sound, or if my fingers don't feel the handle click in the exact right way, my stomach just drops. It just feels wrong. And when it feels wrong, I can't just check the door again and be done with it. I have to pull out my phone, delete all the pictures and videos I just took, and completely restart the entire check from the very beginning. 

And I know I keep repeating myself, but it's just... it's so intense because I'm out there doing this, desperately trying to get that perfect feeling, even when my passengers are standing literally right there on the sidewalk waiting for me. I can see them out there sighing and checking their watches and glaring at me. I know I'm already late. I know I'm making it worse every single time I start the loop over. But if that picture isn't perfect, or if that door doesn't shut just right, I just keep circling the cab, checking the lights and the meter and everything else all over again. I just physically cannot let them in the car until the whole routine feels exactly right.
Are there any areas of your life where these thoughts and safety checks are not causing you any problems or distress?

I mean, didn't you just ask me that? Like, about if there's any part of my life where I can function normally? Because, honestly, no. There's really not. I mean, I can't think of a single place or time where I'm just... free of it. 

Like I was saying, it ruins work, it ruins my studying for my CDL, it ruins hanging out with my friends... it's just always there. Even when I'm just sitting at home, trying to eat dinner or something, my mind is just racing back to the cab. Did I leave the doors unlocked? Did I miss a spot on the tires? What if someone broke in and messed with the brakes because I didn't check the locks perfectly? It just never stops. 

So, no, I don't think there's any area where it's not causing me distress. It's like... it's like this heavy blanket that's just thrown over my entire life, and I can't get out from under it. I can't even sleep right because I'll wake up in a panic, thinking about the safety check from three days ago, wondering if I really heard the door click right or if I just imagined it. It's exhausting. It's completely exhausting, and there's nowhere I can go to just escape it for even five minutes.
Are these thoughts and safety checks significantly interfering with your ability to maintain relationships or perform daily tasks?

I feel like we're just going in circles here, doc, because I feel like I've literally just answered this exact same question twice now. But, I mean, yeah, yes, it absolutely interferes with everything. Like I've been saying, it's completely tearing my life apart. 

I've lost rides, actual paying passengers, because they just give up waiting for me and call an Uber. I've gotten official warnings from dispatch—like, actual written warnings—because I just physically cannot get on the road on time. I'm stuck in the lot, doing the checks, over and over. And then, because I'm so far behind, I'm out there grinding late into the night just to make up the money I lost, which means my studying for my CDL just keeps getting pushed back. And that's my ticket out of here, you know? Getting that commercial license is everything to me, but so much of my day just gets completely eaten up by these checking delays that I never even open the manual. 

And relationships? Forget about it. I barely see my friends anymore. They text me to play games or hang out, and I just have to ignore them or make up an excuse. I can't go because I'm either way behind on my work quota, or I'm just so mentally drained from trying to catch up on everything else in my life after losing hours to the checking. So, yeah, it interferes with every single daily task and relationship I have. I really don't know how else to explain it, it just takes over everything.
Do you feel like these thoughts about the safety checks are in line with your own beliefs and values, or do they feel alien to you?

Alien. Yeah, definitely alien. They don't feel like *me* at all. Honestly, that's the whole reason I finally came in to see someone in the first place. Because... look, I'm a rational guy, right? I know how to do my job. But even when I *know*, for an absolute fact, that I did my safety check—like, I literally just watched my own hands test the doors, I know I did it—this... this thought just comes out of nowhere and completely broadsides me. 

It just keeps hitting me, over and over, that I missed something on the cab. And it's not just a passing "oh, did I forget that?" kind of thought. It's this loud, screaming panic that somebody is going to get seriously hurt because I messed up. Like a tire is gonna blow on the highway and cause a massive wreck, or my boss is gonna find some tiny issue I missed and say I lied on my inspection report and just fire me on the spot. 

And the thing is, I don't actually *believe* I missed anything in my logical brain, but the thought just will not stop. I can't make it shut up. I'll be driving a fare, trying to navigate traffic and just do my job, and my brain is just screaming at me about the brake lines. Or I'll be sitting at my desk later, trying to study for my CDL—which, like I said, is my whole future—and I end up just staring at the exact same paragraph for an hour because this voice in my head keeps playing out these scenarios where my boss is yelling at me for lying about the safety check. It's totally alien to who I actually am. It's like my brain is being hijacked, and I just... I can't turn the volume down, no matter how hard I try to reason with myself. So, no, it doesn't align with my values at all. I hate it.
Are these thoughts and safety checks making it difficult for you to live a normal life and do the things you want to do?

Doc, I... I really feel like you're messing with me right now. Are you reading off a checklist or something? Because this is literally the exact same thing I just told you like two minutes ago. But, I mean, yeah. Yes. A normal life is completely out the window. 

Like I just said, I can't do any of the things I want to do. Take my CDL, for example. I want to drive commercial, I want to get out of driving a taxi, that's my whole goal. But my studying just keeps getting pushed back and pushed back. So much of my day gets completely eaten up by these checking delays that by the time I have a free second, I'm just dead. And work... I mean, I've lost actual rides. Paying customers just cancel on me because I can't get on the road on time, because I'm stuck in the lot checking the tires and the door locks over and over again. I've gotten actual, official warnings from dispatch about it. If I keep it up, I'm gonna lose the only job I have.

And a normal life for a nineteen-year-old usually means having a social life, right? But I barely see my friends anymore. I just can't. I'm either way behind on my work and having to drive crazy late hours to make up for the fares I lost, or I'm just spending my whole night trying to catch up on everything else after the checking delays ruined my schedule for the day. So, yeah, it's making it difficult. I'm not living a normal life at all. I honestly don't even know what a normal day looks like anymore, because every single day is just a fight with my own brain just to get out of the parking lot.
Are these thoughts and safety checks affecting your daily life or relationships in any way that you feel is significant or unbearable?

Are you... are you serious right now? I mean, doc, I don't want to be disrespectful, but are you actually listening to a single word I'm saying? Because I feel like I'm losing my mind here. This is literally the exact same question you've asked me three times in a row now. Just reworded. It's like you're reading from a script and just cycling through variations of "does this bother you?" 

Yes. Yes, it is unbearable. It is completely, 100% significant and unbearable. I literally just laid it all out for you, but I guess I'll say it again. My daily life is a wreck. I drive a taxi, right? And I've lost actual paying rides—people who are standing there waiting for me, and they just cancel and get an Uber because I physically cannot get my cab out of the lot on time. I'm stuck there, checking the doors, checking the tires, over and over and over, and the clock is just ticking. And because of that, my dispatch has given me actual, written warnings. Like, my job is on the line here. If I lose this job, I have nothing. 

And then there's my CDL. I want to drive commercial trucks. That's my ticket to a better life, that's my whole plan for my future. But I can't even open the study manual. I can't. Because so much of my day is completely eaten up by these checking delays, and then I have to stay out driving crazy late hours just to make up for the fares I lost in the morning, that by the time I get home, I'm just completely fried. The studying just keeps getting pushed back, day after day after day. 

And my relationships? My friends? I mean, what friends at this point? I barely see them anymore. They want to hang out, they want to play games, and I just can't do it. I'm either way behind on my work quota because I lost two hours in the parking lot that morning, or I'm just spending my entire night trying to catch up on basic life stuff because the checking delays completely ruined my schedule. I have no social life. I have no free time. I have no peace. It affects absolutely everything, every single day, and I really, really don't know how else to explain to you how unbearable it is. Do you understand what I'm saying this time? Because I can't keep answering the same question.
Do you think that if you didn't perform these safety checks, something bad would definitely happen, or is it more about the anxiety and uncertainty you feel when you haven't done them?

Honestly, it's... it's the uncertainty. I mean, like I said, logically I know the car is probably fine. I know a tire isn't just going to spontaneously explode if I don't look at it for a fifth time. target_item.manifestation: Before I can take a ride, I keep going around the car checking the tires, lights, doors, meter, and paperwork over and over, sometimes taking pictures and restarting the whole check if it doesn't feel right, even when passengers are waiting and I'm already late.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the need for things to be symmetrical or 'just right', which directly relates to my compulsion of restarting the safety check if it doesn't 'feel right'.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean, I kind of touched on that a minute ago, but yes, absolutely. It is one hundred percent about that feeling. It has to feel exactly right, or I can't move on. Like I was saying before about my routine before I can take a ride... I keep going around the car, checking the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, and the paperwork over and over again, right? Well, the reason I get stuck doing it over and over is exactly because of that "just right" thing you just mentioned. 

If I take a picture of the tire tread, for example, and my hand shakes even a tiny bit, or the streetlamp casts a weird shadow across the rubber, it doesn't feel right. Or the doors—man, the doors are the absolute worst. If I shut the back passenger door and it doesn't make this specific, solid sound, or if my fingers don't feel the handle click in the exact right way, my stomach just drops. It just feels wrong. And when it feels wrong, I can't just check the door again and be done with it. I have to pull out my phone, delete all the pictures and videos I just took, and completely restart the entire check from the very beginning. 

And I know I keep repeating myself, but it's just... it's so intense because I'm out there doing this, desperately trying to get that perfect feeling, even when my passengers are standing literally right there on the sidewalk waiting for me. I can see them out there sighing and checking their watches and glaring at me. I know I'm already late. I know I'm making it worse every single time I start the loop over. But if that picture isn't perfect, or if that door doesn't shut just right, I just keep circling the cab, checking the lights and the meter and everything else all over again. I just physically cannot let them in the car until the whole routine feels exactly right.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life
doctor.question: Are there any areas of your life where these thoughts and safety checks are not causing you any problems or distress?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about areas of life where the thoughts and safety checks do not cause problems or distress. This is essentially asking about the absence of functional impairment or distress, which the patient already answered in a previous turn (stating there are no normal areas left). The question is a repetition/rephrasing of the functional impairment inquiry, but there is no new symptom profile item to cover this, and functional impairment has already been addressed.

patient.answer:
I mean, didn't you just ask me that? Like, about if there's any part of my life where I can function normally? Because, honestly, no. There's really not. I mean, I can't think of a single place or time where I'm just... free of it. 

Like I was saying, it ruins work, it ruins my studying for my CDL, it ruins hanging out with my friends... it's just always there. Even when I'm just sitting at home, trying to eat dinner or something, my mind is just racing back to the cab. Did I leave the doors unlocked? Did I miss a spot on the tires? What if someone broke in and messed with the brakes because I didn't check the locks perfectly? It just never stops. 

So, no, I don't think there's any area where it's not causing me distress. It's like... it's like this heavy blanket that's just thrown over my entire life, and I can't get out from under it. I can't even sleep right because I'll wake up in a panic, thinking about the safety check from three days ago, wondering if I really heard the door click right or if I just imagined it. It's exhausting. It's completely exhausting, and there's nowhere I can go to just escape it for even five minutes.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life
doctor.question: Are these thoughts and safety checks significantly interfering with your ability to maintain relationships or perform daily tasks?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I've lost rides and gotten warnings because I can't get on the road on time, and my CDL studying keeps getting pushed back because so much of my day gets eaten up. I barely see friends anymore because I'm either behind on work or trying to catch up after the checking delays.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the thoughts and safety checks are significantly interfering with the patient's ability to maintain relationships or perform daily tasks, which directly addresses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I feel like we're just going in circles here, doc, because I feel like I've literally just answered this exact same question twice now. But, I mean, yeah, yes, it absolutely interferes with everything. Like I've been saying, it's completely tearing my life apart. 

I've lost rides, actual paying passengers, because they just give up waiting for me and call an Uber. I've gotten official warnings from dispatch—like, actual written warnings—because I just physically cannot get on the road on time. I'm stuck in the lot, doing the checks, over and over. And then, because I'm so far behind, I'm out there grinding late into the night just to make up the money I lost, which means my studying for my CDL just keeps getting pushed back. And that's my ticket out of here, you know? Getting that commercial license is everything to me, but so much of my day just gets completely eaten up by these checking delays that I never even open the manual. 

And relationships? Forget about it. I barely see my friends anymore. They text me to play games or hang out, and I just have to ignore them or make up an excuse. I can't go because I'm either way behind on my work quota, or I'm just so mentally drained from trying to catch up on everything else in my life after losing hours to the checking. So, yeah, it interferes with every single daily task and relationship I have. I really don't know how else to explain it, it just takes over everything.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's thoughts are ego-dystonic
doctor.question: Do you feel like these thoughts about the safety checks are in line with your own beliefs and values, or do they feel alien to you?

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because even when I know I did my safety check, this thought keeps hitting me that I missed something on the cab and somebody could get hurt or my boss will say I lied, and I can't make it shut up while I'm driving or trying to study.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the thoughts are ego-dystonic (feel alien/unwanted vs in line with beliefs), which is a core characteristic of obsessions.

patient.answer:
Alien. Yeah, definitely alien. They don't feel like *me* at all. Honestly, that's the whole reason I finally came in to see someone in the first place. Because... look, I'm a rational guy, right? I know how to do my job. But even when I *know*, for an absolute fact, that I did my safety check—like, I literally just watched my own hands test the doors, I know I did it—this... this thought just comes out of nowhere and completely broadsides me. 

It just keeps hitting me, over and over, that I missed something on the cab. And it's not just a passing "oh, did I forget that?" kind of thought. It's this loud, screaming panic that somebody is going to get seriously hurt because I messed up. Like a tire is gonna blow on the highway and cause a massive wreck, or my boss is gonna find some tiny issue I missed and say I lied on my inspection report and just fire me on the spot. 

And the thing is, I don't actually *believe* I missed anything in my logical brain, but the thought just will not stop. I can't make it shut up. I'll be driving a fare, trying to navigate traffic and just do my job, and my brain is just screaming at me about the brake lines. Or I'll be sitting at my desk later, trying to study for my CDL—which, like I said, is my whole future—and I end up just staring at the exact same paragraph for an hour because this voice in my head keeps playing out these scenarios where my boss is yelling at me for lying about the safety check. It's totally alien to who I actually am. It's like my brain is being hijacked, and I just... I can't turn the volume down, no matter how hard I try to reason with myself. So, no, it doesn't align with my values at all. I hate it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life
doctor.question: Are these thoughts and safety checks making it difficult for you to live a normal life and do the things you want to do?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I've lost rides and gotten warnings because I can't get on the road on time, and my CDL studying keeps getting pushed back because so much of my day gets eaten up. I barely see friends anymore because I'm either behind on work or trying to catch up after the checking delays.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the thoughts and safety checks are making it difficult to live a normal life and do desired activities, which directly relates to functional impairment, such as losing rides, getting warnings, delaying studying, and not seeing friends.

patient.answer:
Doc, I... I really feel like you're messing with me right now. Are you reading off a checklist or something? Because this is literally the exact same thing I just told you like two minutes ago. But, I mean, yeah. Yes. A normal life is completely out the window. 

Like I just said, I can't do any of the things I want to do. Take my CDL, for example. I want to drive commercial, I want to get out of driving a taxi, that's my whole goal. But my studying just keeps getting pushed back and pushed back. So much of my day gets completely eaten up by these checking delays that by the time I have a free second, I'm just dead. And work... I mean, I've lost actual rides. Paying customers just cancel on me because I can't get on the road on time, because I'm stuck in the lot checking the tires and the door locks over and over again. I've gotten actual, official warnings from dispatch about it. If I keep it up, I'm gonna lose the only job I have.

And a normal life for a nineteen-year-old usually means having a social life, right? But I barely see my friends anymore. I just can't. I'm either way behind on my work and having to drive crazy late hours to make up for the fares I lost, or I'm just spending my whole night trying to catch up on everything else after the checking delays ruined my schedule for the day. So, yeah, it's making it difficult. I'm not living a normal life at all. I honestly don't even know what a normal day looks like anymore, because every single day is just a fight with my own brain just to get out of the parking lot.

doctor.question: Are these thoughts and safety checks affecting your daily life or relationships in any way that you feel is significant or unbearable?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I've lost rides and gotten warnings because I can't get on the road on time, and my CDL studying keeps getting pushed back because so much of my day gets eaten up. I barely see friends anymore because I'm either behind on work or trying to catch up after the checking delays.
target_item.reason: The doctor is again asking about how the symptoms are affecting daily life and relationships, which corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Are you... are you serious right now? I mean, doc, I don't want to be disrespectful, but are you actually listening to a single word I'm saying? Because I feel like I'm losing my mind here. This is literally the exact same question you've asked me three times in a row now. Just reworded. It's like you're reading from a script and just cycling through variations of "does this bother you?" 

Yes. Yes, it is unbearable. It is completely, 100% significant and unbearable. I literally just laid it all out for you, but I guess I'll say it again. My daily life is a wreck. I drive a taxi, right? And I've lost actual paying rides—people who are standing there waiting for me, and they just cancel and get an Uber because I physically cannot get my cab out of the lot on time. I'm stuck there, checking the doors, checking the tires, over and over and over, and the clock is just ticking. And because of that, my dispatch has given me actual, written warnings. Like, my job is on the line here. If I lose this job, I have nothing. 

And then there's my CDL. I want to drive commercial trucks. That's my ticket to a better life, that's my whole plan for my future. But I can't even open the study manual. I can't. Because so much of my day is completely eaten up by these checking delays, and then I have to stay out driving crazy late hours just to make up for the fares I lost in the morning, that by the time I get home, I'm just completely fried. The studying just keeps getting pushed back, day after day after day. 

And my relationships? My friends? I mean, what friends at this point? I barely see them anymore. They want to hang out, they want to play games, and I just can't do it. I'm either way behind on my work quota because I lost two hours in the parking lot that morning, or I'm just spending my entire night trying to catch up on basic life stuff because the checking delays completely ruined my schedule. I have no social life. I have no free time. I have no peace. It affects absolutely everything, every single day, and I really, really don't know how else to explain to you how unbearable it is. Do you understand what I'm saying this time? Because I can't keep answering the same question.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are more aligned with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) or generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)
doctor.question: Do you think that if you didn't perform these safety checks, something bad would definitely happen, or is it more about the anxiety and uncertainty you feel when you haven't done them?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: Before I can take a ride, I keep going around the car checking the tires, lights, doors, meter, and paperwork over and over, sometimes taking pictures and restarting the whole check if it doesn't feel right, even when passengers are waiting and I'm already late.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the motivation behind the safety checks (whether to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce anxiety/uncertainty), which is the core defining feature of compulsions.

patient.answer:
Honestly, it's... it's the uncertainty. I mean, like I said, logically I know the car is probably fine. I know a tire isn't just going to spontaneously explode if I don't look at it for a fifth time. But the anxiety and the not knowing for absolute, 100% sure? That's what completely paralyzes me. It's this overwhelming feeling of doubt that just builds and builds until I physically cannot do anything else until I've done my routine to make the feeling go away. 

And the routine itself is just... it's exhausting. Before I can even take a ride, before I can even put the cab in drive, I have to get out and go around the car. And it's not just a quick glance. I'm checking the tires, I'm checking all the lights, I'm testing the doors to make sure they're secure, I'm checking the meter inside, and I'm flipping through all my paperwork over and over again. And the worst part is, it has to feel *right*. If I'm halfway through—say I'm checking the back right door—and suddenly my brain goes, "Wait, did you really look at the front left tire? Are you sure?"... I can't just go check the tire. I have to completely restart the whole entire check from the very beginning. 

I've even gotten to the point where I'm taking pictures with my phone. Like, I'll take a photo of the paperwork or the door locks just so I have proof that I checked them, but then I'll just end up standing there staring at the photo, zooming in on it, wondering if I missed something in the background of the picture. And I'll be doing all of this, just circling the car, restarting the checks, taking photos, while there are literally passengers waiting for me. Like, I can see them standing on the curb, looking at their phones, getting annoyed because I'm already late to pick them up, and I just can't stop. I want to stop, I know they're waiting, I know I'm losing money, but the uncertainty is so loud that I just keep going around and around the car until it finally feels okay.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of repetitive safety checks, intrusive thoughts about potential disasters, and a strong need for symmetry and perfection in their checks are characteristic of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). The patient's distress and impairment in daily life, including work, studying, and social relationships, further support this diagnosis.
